Gemma Edge AI Hackathon Winners Shipped with Google LiteRT and NVIDIA Jetson at AGI House

Community Article Published
November 24, 2026 Upvote 6 AGI House Labs AGI-House litert-community SB codeandsomedata litert-community Aditya Sahu adsahu-nv litert-community

Four projects from the Google Gemma Hardware Hackathon show what builders can create with local inference on LiteRT, and NVIDIA Jetson.
On October 24, 2026, AGI House and Google DeepMind hosted the Google Gemma Hardware Hackathon, bringing together 100+ builders to bring on-device intelligence to real hardware in a single day. Builders worked across a wide range of edge hardware from our partners, including NVIDIA Jetson, Qualcomm, Google Pixel and Android, Raspberry Pi, Arduino and Synaptics, and submitted 40 projects by the end of the day.
AGI House is a frontier AI community, applied lab and venture fund based in Hillsborough, California. Throughout the year, we host build days that bring researchers, founders and engineers together to build with the newest models and tools.
The day opened with talks from the Google LiteRT and NVIDIA Jetson teams. Builders then formed teams and spent the afternoon turning ideas into working demos, with one constraint: projects had to run entirely on-device.
The projects covered a wide range of problems. The four featured below include an offline guide for hikers, a hands-free music app, a language learning app for children and a fault-tolerant robotics system. Several teams combined more than one device in a single system, splitting the work across phones, workstations and robots. The projects were recognized in two tracks: Best Use of LiteRT and NVIDIA’s Choice.

Build On-Device with LiteRT

LiteRT is Google’s runtime for running machine learning models directly on devices, from phones and laptops to embedded hardware. It helps developers make efficient use of CPUs, GPUs, and supported neural processing units. For large language models like Gemma, LiteRT-LM builds on that runtime to handle tasks such as managing conversation state and generating responses.
Running a model where the data is created changes what developers can build. An app can respond without waiting for a network round trip, keep sensitive inputs on the device, and work when connectivity is unreliable or unavailable. Local inference can reduce cloud costs for features people use frequently.
At the Google Gemma Hardware Hackathon, hosted by Google DeepMind and AGI House, our team was excited to see what builders would make when their projects had to run entirely on-device. Three projects recognized for their use of LiteRT showed how different those ideas could be. Sherpa Survival built an offline guide for hikers, where a reliable connection is hard to count on. DJemma used head movements to let people control their phones and make music. Wonder Agent brought on-device AI to a learning experience for kids.
What stood out to us was how naturally the technology fit each problem. A hiker needs guidance where there’s no signal. A hands-free interface needs to respond as you move. And a learning app can process a child’s interactions locally. Seeing builders turn those needs into working demos in a day was the part we were most excited about.

NVIDIA × LiteRT collaboration

NVIDIA Jetson is a compute platform for physical AI, bringing accelerated computing to robots and autonomous machines that perceive, reason, and act in the real world. By running AI locally, NVIDIA Jetson enables developers to connect language understanding, vision, and sensor processing with responsive physical interaction. Its support for a broad ecosystem of open models including Google’s powerful Gemma family gives builders the flexibility to bring advances in generative AI directly onto their devices.
Google LiteRT lets developers run AI models locally on NVIDIA Jetson, using WebGPU over Vulkan to accelerate supported workloads on the NVIDIA GPU. Together, LiteRT and NVIDIA Jetson give builders the tools and compute to bring on-device AI into their applications, with attention to response time, memory use, and power consumption.
NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor gives developers the compute to run language and vision models alongside live sensor data, helping them build physical AI systems that understand and interact with the world around them. At the Google Gemma Hardware Hackathon, teams explored what they could build with open models running locally on real hardware. To start building, explore Jetson AI Lab for tutorials, optimized models, and community projects that bring generative AI to NVIDIA Jetson. The projects below share what they built and learned along the way.

Featured projects

NVIDIA’s Choice: Robots with Redundant Inference

Team: Darin Djapri, Bryce Hackel, Ellia Cavanaugh, Kevin Hao

Our project explores a fault-tolerant, fully local AI system that distributes Gemma 4 inference across heterogeneous devices, enabling seamless mid-generation failover when a machine crashes. Using leader election and context reconstruction, the team reports a 625 ms mid-generation handoff in its Ollama-based setup, including a 600 ms failure-detection timeout. We demonstrate the system on a robot arm that autonomously identifies, organizes, and retrieves lab tools using vision-language reasoning running on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor.
Read the team’s story | Watch the demo | Explore the code

Best Use of LiteRT: Sherpa AI

Team: An Sung, Anirudh Kulkarni, Chengjiang Long, Grace Huang

Sherpa Survival is an offline Android and iOS hiking assistant built in Flutter that uses Gemma 4 E2B-it and LiteRT to provide trail navigation, visual identification, and survival guidance without an internet connection. The app pairs local GPS path tracking and trail routing with a four-model native pipeline handling speech-to-text, intent routing, multimodal reasoning, and text-to-speech. Moving forward, the team plans to expand the app with richer offline trail maps and improved retrieval systems beyond Yosemite.
Read the team’s story | Watch the demo | Explore the code

Best Use of LiteRT: DJemma

Team: Dima Dobrynin

DJemma is a hands-free Android music app that lets users play melodies and shape sounds through head movements and facial expressions. At the same time, Gemma 4 adapts the backing music entirely on-device. Beyond music, the same approach can extend to other apps, combining expressive, hands-free controls with local assistance powered by Gemma 4 to enable private, offline, and accessible experiences.
Read the team’s story | Watch the demo | Explore the code

Best Use of LiteRT: Wonder Agent

Team: Frank Du

Wonder Agent is a language education app that helps children learn English words through pictures, voice, and interactive conversation. It runs Gemma and speech inference entirely on the device after setup. Our vision is to bring the marginal cost of education closer to zero through on-device AI. We use LiteRT for local inference and used a GPU workstation (NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada Generation) to prepare 5 models for LiteRT Runtime and generate 10,000 images for our hackathon presentation.
